name: Arginine (AAKG)

card.summary: Arginine alpha-ketoglutarate, a pre-workout 'pump' supplement whose small human trials mostly report no performance benefit.
card.note: Often sold inside stimulant-heavy pre-workouts; a case report links one such product to hemorrhagic stroke.

quick.overview:
AAKG is a salt of the amino acid L-arginine and alpha-ketoglutarate, marketed to lifters as a nitric oxide booster for muscle pumps, blood flow and endurance. It is a staple of pre-workout formulas.

Published human trials are few and small. Titles of several of them report that acute AAKG or arginine supplementation failed to improve muscular performance or endurance.
quick.mechanism: Arginine is the precursor of nitric oxide, which relaxes blood vessels. The marketing idea is that more arginine means more nitric oxide, more blood flow and a bigger pump. Alpha-ketoglutarate is a metabolic intermediate and glutamine precursor. Whether the combined salt raises nitric oxide better than plain arginine is not clearly established.
quick.risks: Grokipedia describes AAKG as generally tolerated at 3 to 6 g daily, with mild gastrointestinal upset at higher intakes. A 2012 case report described a hemorrhagic stroke in a young man after a multi-ingredient sports supplement (Jack3d) that contained other stimulants, so the cause cannot be attributed to AAKG alone.

lead: Arginine alpha-ketoglutarate (AAKG) is a dietary supplement made by pairing the amino acid L-arginine with alpha-ketoglutaric acid, typically in a 2:1 molar ratio, and marketed as more soluble or bioavailable than arginine alone.[1] Lifters and bodybuilders take it, usually inside a pre-workout formula, to chase a bigger muscle 'pump', fuller-looking muscles during training, better blood flow to working muscle and, in the marketing, harder or longer training that adds up to a more muscular physique.[1][11]

The rationale is vascular. Arginine is the only precursor from which the body makes nitric oxide, a gas that relaxes the smooth muscle in blood vessel walls and widens them.[2] More substrate is supposed to mean more nitric oxide, more flow and a more pronounced pump. Alpha-ketoglutarate is an intermediate of the citric acid cycle and a precursor of glutamine, which supporters say helps with energy and ammonia handling.[10][1]

Published human work consists of small trials, many in resistance-trained men. Several report that acute AAKG or arginine supplementation did not change muscular performance or endurance, while a pharmacokinetic study characterised how plasma arginine rises after a dose.[3][4][5] Arginine is also studied outside the gym, in blood pressure, erectile function and wound healing, and is sold in hair-care products.[2][12][13]

chain: AAKG supplies arginine, the precursor of nitric oxide
Proposed wider blood vessels and more blood flow to trained muscle
Bigger-looking pump during training and, proponents hope, better workouts and recovery
angle.text: Lifters take AAKG before training to look and feel fuller in the muscles being worked and to support training quality. The pump is a temporary, in-session effect; any longer-term muscle benefit depends on whether training itself improves, which small trials of AAKG have not shown.

paras: AAKG is sold as a stand-alone powder or capsule and as an ingredient in multi-ingredient pre-workout products. Proponents say it supports muscle pumps during resistance training, aids recovery and promotes ammonia handling through the urea cycle.[1] Pre-workout blends, according to Wikipedia, are usually proprietary mixtures averaging around 18 ingredients, with caffeine nearly universal, and arginine and citrulline are the standard 'pump' ingredients.[11]

The related supplement citrulline, often sold as citrulline malate, is the by-product of nitric oxide synthesis and is used as an alternative or add-on to arginine; Wikipedia notes it is promoted for athletic performance and remains under preliminary research.[20][11]

L-arginine is a semi-essential amino acid. Nitric oxide synthases convert it into nitric oxide, identified as the endothelium-derived relaxing factor, which diffuses into smooth muscle, activates guanylate cyclase and dilates vessels. Asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) inhibits this reaction and is regarded as a marker of vascular disease.[2] Healthy people usually make enough arginine themselves, and it is also found in meat, dairy, eggs, seeds, nuts and legumes.[2]

Alpha-ketoglutaric acid is a dicarboxylic acid that sits in the citric acid cycle, is produced when glutamine is broken down, helps move excess nitrogen toward the urea cycle, and serves as a cofactor for several enzyme families.[10] Wikipedia notes that much of the research on supplemental alpha-ketoglutarate is preclinical, with longevity findings in worms and mice and one uncontrolled 2021 human study of a multi-ingredient product, and that no randomized controlled trials show pharmacological effects of it in humans.[10] A 1997 study in burn-injured rats compared arginine alpha-ketoglutarate with ornithine alpha-ketoglutarate for glutamine pools.[15] Grokipedia states that neither plain arginine nor AAKG has been shown superior for nitric oxide production or muscle outcomes.[1]
A pharmacokinetic study in 10 healthy men compared 4 g of time-released and non-time-released AAKG and tracked plasma arginine over 8 hours.[5]

A 2006 report in Nutrition described two randomized, double-blind studies in trained men that evaluated AAKG's pharmacokinetics, safety and effects on exercise.[5] A 2008 study examined a creatine, AAKG, amino acid and medium-chain triglyceride combination for endurance and performance, which cannot separate the effect of AAKG from the other ingredients.[14]

A 2011 trial reported that acute arginine supplementation did not improve muscle endurance or alter blood pressure responses to resistance exercise, and a 2012 trial reported that acute AAKG supplementation failed to improve muscular performance in resistance-trained and untrained men.[4][3] Another 2011 study examined seven days of AAKG on blood flow, plasma arginine and nitric oxide metabolites after resistance exercise.[6]

Two 2017 studies tested a multi-ingredient pre-workout product, with and without synephrine, on acute exercise outcomes and on eight weeks of training adaptations in resistance-trained males; because the product contains many ingredients, effects cannot be assigned to AAKG alone.[7][8] The training-adaptations study was registered as NCT02999581 with 122 participants.[16]

Outside exercise, a 2019 meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials (540 men with mild to moderate erectile dysfunction) examined arginine supplements and reported improvement compared with placebo or no treatment, and a 2021 meta-analysis examined arginine and glutamine for wound healing.[12][13] These concern plain arginine and different outcomes.

Grokipedia reports that AAKG is generally well tolerated at 3 to 6 g daily, with nausea or diarrhea at higher intakes, and that it is not recommended for people with herpes infections or kidney problems.[1] Wikipedia lists plain L-arginine as generally recognized as safe at intakes up to 20 g per day and notes possible interactions with prescription drugs and herbal supplements.[2]

A 2012 military medicine case report described a hemorrhagic stroke in a young healthy man after use of the multi-ingredient sports supplement Jack3d.[9] Wikipedia notes that the FDA banned DMAA, a stimulant that had been a common pre-workout ingredient in products such as Jack3d, in 2012 over concerns about chest pain and heart attack, so the case involved a product with other stimulants and cannot be attributed to AAKG alone.[11] Wikipedia also reports that the FDA has limited power over supplements, that the maker is responsible for safety, and that undeclared ingredients have been found in some pre-workout products.[11]

Arginine was first isolated in 1886 from yellow lupin seedlings by Ernst Schulze and Ernst Steiger, with its structure determined in 1897 and synthesised in 1899.[2] Pre-workout supplements trace to 1982, when Dan Duchaine created Ultimate Orange in Venice, California; by the early 2000s arginine and citrulline were being sold in blends for a temporary muscle pump, and the market grew from about $2.7 billion in 2008 to about $14.2 billion in 2022.[11]

AAKG became a common labelled ingredient in bodybuilding products during that period. Discussion on T Nation includes threads on peri-workout nutrition and supplement stacks where arginine products are discussed among other supplements.[17][18]

Looksmaxxing forums mention arginine less for muscle than for hair and growth. One looksmax.org thread discusses an arginine-containing hair strengthening spray sold by a supermarket chain, whose label says it nourishes hair, thickens it and makes it grow faster, and whose original poster asked whether it was credible.[19] Arginine is also marketed as a growth hormone booster, which is the basis of height questions about it; Wikipedia's arginine article reports one review in which oral arginine raised GH and a later trial in which it raised plasma arginine but not GH.[2]

timeline.event: Ernst Schulze and Ernst Steiger isolate arginine from yellow lupin seedlings.[2]
Dan Duchaine creates Ultimate Orange, regarded as the first pre-workout supplement.[11]
Rat study compares arginine alpha-ketoglutarate with ornithine alpha-ketoglutarate in burn injury.[15]
Pharmacokinetics, safety and exercise effects of AAKG reported in trained men.[5]
Trials of acute arginine and of seven days of AAKG report on endurance and blood flow after resistance exercise.[4][6]

Two studies test a multi-ingredient pre-workout supplement over acute and eight-week periods.[7][8]
Meta-analysis of arginine supplements for erectile dysfunction published.[12]

lore.intro: AAKG sits inside the pre-workout and pump-supplement culture of bodybuilding forums; on looksmaxxing forums arginine also comes up for hair and growth questions.[17][19]

claims.claim: AAKG gives bigger muscle pumps by boosting nitric oxide.
claims.believers: Supplement makers and users say more arginine means more nitric oxide, wider vessels and fuller muscles during training.[1][11]
claims.experts: Arginine is the precursor of nitric oxide, but trials of acute arginine or AAKG have reported no improvement in muscular performance or endurance, and Grokipedia states no clear superiority over plain arginine has been shown.[2][3][4][1]

claims.claim: AAKG improves strength, endurance and training results.
claims.believers: Marketing for AAKG products lists strength and endurance gains and recovery support.[1]
claims.experts: A 2012 trial found acute AAKG did not improve muscular performance in resistance-trained and untrained men, and a 2011 trial found acute arginine did not improve muscle endurance.[3][4]

claims.claim: AAKG is better absorbed than plain arginine.
claims.believers: Sellers describe the salt as more soluble and bioavailable.[1]
claims.experts: A pharmacokinetic study tracked plasma arginine after AAKG in 10 men, and Grokipedia states neither form has been shown clearly better for nitric oxide or muscle outcomes.[5][1]

claims.claim: Arginine boosts growth hormone, and so height or muscle.
claims.believers: Supplement marketing presents arginine as a growth hormone booster, and some users ask whether that could matter for height or muscle.[11]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that in one trial oral arginine raised plasma arginine but not growth hormone.[2]

claims.claim: Arginine in hair products thickens hair and speeds growth.
claims.believers: A supermarket hair spray's label, quoted on looksmax.org, says its arginine nourishes, thickens and speeds growth, and the poster started using it.[19]
claims.experts: No published trial of arginine for scalp hair growth appears in the research on arginine, which covers exercise, blood pressure, erectile function and wound healing.[2][12][13]

claims.claim: Pre-workout products containing AAKG are risky.
claims.believers: Some lifters report heart-racing or headaches from stimulant-heavy blends.[11]
claims.experts: A 2012 case report links a stroke to the multi-ingredient product Jack3d, and the FDA banned DMAA in 2012; the products contained other stimulants.[9][11]
